status: preliminary, original live run; corrected harness not rerun
interpretation_html:
Correction after inspecting the failures

Most rounds had the wrong window distribution

The saved window states prove that both Rift rounds and yabai round 2 placed all six disposable windows on workspace 5. The intended setup was three on workspace 5 and three on workspace 6. The harness checked the total count and missed the distribution.

Only yabai round 1 has the intended distribution in its recorded state. The earlier pooled 9.3× expansion comparison is not a valid equal-workload benchmark. The original measurements remain below, but their ratios and pass rates cannot establish an engine ranking.

Your direct observation of Rift reshuffling windows one at a time remains valid. The implementation does float and reinsert other tiles sequentially, and these attempts took roughly two seconds. Keeping yabai is the practical choice for your established workflow; the current data does not justify replacing it for performance or resource savings.

Recorded command times, for diagnosis only

__SUMMARY_TABLE__

These medians pool the original attempts, including invalid setups. They describe what happened, not equivalent-workload performance. Passing means the old predicate matched; it is not proof of the intended behavior.

What caused yabai's red checks?

CheckEvidenceDisposition
Workspace switch: 6 failuresAll targeted workspace 6 in round 2, while both fixture apps were on workspace 5. Round 1 passed all 12 switches.Invalid fixture expectation. Not evidence of a normal yabai focus regression. The preceding setup/launch placement needs a separate investigation.
Cross-monitor focus: 1 failureRound 2 expected focus on a fixture app on the right monitor; that app was actually on workspace 5.Invalid fixture expectation.
Cross-monitor move: 1 failureRound 2 expected an incoming half-width tile among three destination windows, but workspace 6 was empty. Later left-crossing checks show the window did reach workspace 6.The transfer succeeded; the expected occupied-destination geometry was invalid.
Float restore: 1 failureRound 2, with six windows on one workspace. The original run did not save the failed frame and checked only one matching state.Follow-up confirmed a real float-helper geometry bug and fixed it. The original failed frame was not recorded; see the targeted test below.
Width presets: 3 failuresRound 1's 65%, 75%, then 65% targets failed; returning to 50% passed. Commands completed in 45–59 ms, then the final-state checks waited about four seconds.Unresolved geometry or test-baseline issue, not a speed threshold. These failures occurred in the correctly distributed round and should not be ignored if reproducible.
Follow-up: floating restoration fixed

A real helper bug, reproduced independently

A later focused check used one disposable window and independently read its CoreGraphics bounds. The old helper requested 2032×1106 but left the window at 2540×1382. A move immediately after resize reused stale dimensions and overwrote the requested size.

The helper now waits for position to update, applies the saved size, and confirms the complete frame. It saves fresh floating geometry and serializes overlapping shortcut invocations. There is no new background process.

The user requested a recheck. All six tile/float cycles restored exactly to the two chosen position-and-size combinations. Restore calls took 65.7–70.5 ms in that recheck, including process startup. This is total action time, not a claim of zero added latency. The window was closed and the original workspace restored afterward.

Targeted check data · Upstream full-frame move implementation. This resolves the confirmed floating-helper defect; the three width-preset failures remain unresolved.

Resource observations

Short idle samples showed roughly 0.12% of one CPU core for both managers. Manager RSS averaged 35.0 MB for yabai and 37.4 MB for Rift. With sampled shortcuts/helpers it was 68.4 MB and 66.9 MB.

These are provisional observations over about 16 seconds per manager. Different fixture placement and helper sampling limit comparisons. There is no demonstrated resource benefit large enough to motivate a switch.

Active CPU is not a fair ranking

Recorded service CPU averaged 11.43% for yabai and 9.00% for Rift, but the workloads, durations, failed waits and completed operations differed.

CPU percentages, pooled ratios and energy claims should not guide the decision from this run. Detailed samples are preserved for diagnosis.

Harness corrections, not yet rerun live

  • Require exactly three windows from each fixture app on its assigned workspace before measuring. A placement failure aborts the phase.
  • Give the two fixture apps distinct bundle identities.
  • Require two consecutive matching states; preserve before-state and failed-state geometry.
  • Record an independent macOS focus/geometry observation after each attempt.
  • Verify the 50% preset baseline before stepping through preset sizes.
  • Treat AeroSpace's empty focused-window query as a valid empty state.

No additional live benchmark was run after your request to review the report first. A later targeted floating test confirmed and fixed a helper bug, as documented above. Width presets still need their own diagnostic. The original manager benchmark was not rerun.

Monitor movement follow-up: behavior fixed; speed regression caught

An uncontrollable, non-AX Activity Monitor window was being included as a tiled leaf. Its failed warp left an insertion overlay and skipped restoring focus. The helper now filters these records, follows the moved window before rearranging, and clears failed insertion hints.

The first targeted check passed 16 crossings and four swap/expand sequences. A later pre-insertion check confirmed all 16 observed arrival edges before layout normalization, with focus retained. These are disposable-window checks, not PyCharm-specific validation.

Preselecting the edge was not faster. The separate, uninstrumented pass measured three-window arrivals at 609–776 ms, versus 288–333 ms in the earlier rightward check. Four-window arrivals took 678–759 ms; empty destinations took 174–240 ms. Samples are small and sequential. The instrumented arrival checks pause for observation and are excluded from this timing comparison.

The correction chooses a perpendicular split for two equal destination tiles, retaining the fast mirror/swap path rather than creating narrow columns that need rebuilding. The correction passed 32 crossings and 16 swap/expand sequences, including 16 independently observed arrival edges. Uninstrumented three-window arrivals took 303–396 ms; the rightward median fell about 45% relative to the regression. This is close to the earlier working helper range (288–365 ms), not evidence of a speedup over it. Empty destinations took 174–227 ms; four-window arrivals still took 689–1273 ms. The larger rebuild remains a performance limitation. No idle polling or background service was added. All targeted movement data.

Four-window rebuild optimization: matched before/after check

A guarded grid path moves one neighboring tile and balances only the opposite column. It avoids the extra warp, whole-space balance and order repairs performed by the fallback. Parent split metadata must match the geometry; other shapes retain the existing fallback.

Median crossing time fell from 671 ms to 500 ms, about 25% lower. Native requests fell from 24–25 to 16. The test alternated old and new implementations, with exactly matching initial window assignments and frames in each direction. There were six samples per implementation. These timings exclude helper process startup and should not be pooled with earlier CLI samples.

All 12 matched crossings preserved focus, reading order and balanced sizing. Another 16 crossings and eight swap/expand sequences passed. The initial baseline attempt exposed an overly strict size assertion: native BSP balance applies nested gaps, so equally balanced leaves differ slightly in height. The corrected check applies the same tolerance to both implementations and also rejects overlap.

The speedup applies to the tested grid. Other layouts can still take the slower fallback. Refocusing remains a substantial cost, about 208 ms median on the new path. There is no added background work; this check makes no CPU or memory claim. All samples and per-command timings.
notes: Corrected analysis: both Rift rounds and yabai round 2 have six fixture windows on workspace 5 in the earliest saved states. Their workload and behavior expectations are invalid. Original failed checks and timings are retained for diagnosis, not scored as valid comparisons.
Original raw measurements are preserved unchanged in window-managers-2026-09-16.json. The corrected harness has not been run live; no new benchmark was started after you requested a report first.
The actual operating system is macOS 27.0 build 26A428, despite the initial discussion referring to macOS 26.
Idle sampling was only about 8 seconds per phase, 16 seconds per manager in total. Sub-percentage CPU differences are not a reliable energy ranking.

AeroSpace completed no behavior or resource measurements due to the harness treating an empty focused-window query as fatal. This is a harness setup failure, not an AeroSpace performance result. AeroSpace is outside the current switch decision at your request.

Rift's second run ended during retiling after 52 of the 60 planned cases. Missing cases must not be counted as passes. Successful-only latency numbers are conditional on completing the requested action.

The first fixture used two processes of the same app executable. Separate app identities, two consecutive matching states, failed-state captures and an independent macOS focus observation were added for a future run to investigate possible fixture/focus ambiguity.

The original run saved geometry for passing attempts only. It used manager-reported focus and geometry, except AeroSpace would use CoreGraphics. No screen-recorded frame latency, keyboard-event path, docking, sleep/wake or long-duration stability claim is supported.

A missing subscriber/helper sample does not establish zero resource use. RSS sums count shared pages more than once, and 200ms sampling can miss short-lived processes. Active CPU includes setup/rearrangement between cases and confirmation queries.

The user's visible one-at-a-time expansion observation agrees with the repeated timing result. The current Rift BSP adapter sequentially floats and reinserts other tiles. However, the unequal fixture distribution invalidates the earlier 9.3× equal-workload comparison.

After the benchmark, the user switched to yabai and reported D201 in the bar. Read-only inspection confirmed six correct yabai desktops but stale Rift bar items. This switch/rendering defect was not caught by the benchmark's manager-process checks and is scheduled for repair after report delivery.

Post-report bar repair: reloaded the live yabai renderer and removed stale Rift items. Added a manager-specific readiness marker and post-handoff verification, also applied when selecting the already-active manager. Offline regression tests cover stale callbacks; no additional live manager-switch benchmark was run.

Final configuration: yabai is saved for login. The monitor badge omits Y, alternatives show A/R, and Off denotes no active manager. Menu choices are temporary. Quit stops manager and shortcut processes while retaining the login preference. This command was verified with mocked processes; the live desktop was not stopped for that test.

Follow-up on float restoration: the old helper reproduced incorrect dimensions twice in a one-window test. After sequencing move and resize around observed frame updates, the requested recheck passed six exact position/size restores. See float-restoration-2026-09-16.json. Original benchmark measurements remain unchanged.
